questions.question:
**Directions: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No improvement’.**

While my __parents talked__ to the visitor, I made tea in the kitchen.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'parents were talking'.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• In the given sentence, the use of the simple past tense 'talked' is incorrect.
 
• The given sentence is in the past continuous tense as it is used to describe something that was happening continuously in the past when another action interrupted it.
 
• The **past continuous tense** is formed by **combining** the past tense of to be (**was/were**) with the **verb’s present participle** (**-ing** word).
 
• Therefore, the past continuous tense ''were talking'' should be used **in place of** the simple past tense 'talked'.

 

Hence, the correct answer is option 3.

Correct Sentence: *While my **parents were talking** to the visitor, I made tea in the kitchen*.

questions.question:
**Select the option that will improve the (bracketed) part of the sentence. In case of no improvement select the option 'No improvement'.**

The play was (either as funny or as) disturbing as Shivang told it was.
questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is **Neither as funny nor as.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence **"The play was (either as funny or as) disturbing as Shivang told it was" **contains an error in the use of correlative conjunctions.
 
• **Correlative conjunctions **are used to join words or groups of words that have equal importance in a sentence.
 
• In this case, the correlative conjunction** "either...or" **is incorrectly used. It should be replaced with **"neither...nor" **to convey the intended meaning.
 
• **"Neither...nor"** is **used to present two negative options or choices.**
 
 
• Sentence with the improved option: The play was **neither as funny nor as**__ disturbing as Shivang told it was.
 
 
 
• In this corrected sentence, the use of** "neither...nor"** properly balances the comparison between the play's level of funniness and its level of disturbance. It ensures that both aspects are presented as negative or not as expected.
 
• The other options provided, such as** "either as funny nor as" **and **"neither as funny or as," **are grammatically incorrect and do not convey the intended meaning. Therefore, **option 1, "neither as funny nor as," **is the correct choice.

__**Correct Sentence**__: *The play was __**(neither as funny nor as)**__ disturbing as Shivang told it was.*

The recent cloudburst completely __dismantled__ the village and its people.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Option 3** i.e. **took apart**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"dismantled"** means to take something apart so that it is in separate pieces. (विखंडित करना)

 
 
• **Example: **The workers dismantled the old machinery to make space for the new equipment.
 
 
 
• **"Took apart" **refers to breaking something into its individual components, similar to dismantling. (विखंडित करना)
 
 
• **Example: **He took apart the clock to see how it worked.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 3 i.e. took apart**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Took after **(पर जाना): To resemble a parent or ancestor in appearance or behavior.

 
 
• **Example:** She really took after her mother in terms of talent and looks.
 
 
 
• **Took back **(वापस लेना): To retract or withdraw something said or done.
 
 
• **Example: **He took back his words after realizing he was wrong.
 
 
 
• **Took up** (उठा लिया): To begin a new hobby or activity.
 
 
• **Example:** She took up painting after retiring from her job.

questions.question:

You have locked the gate, __isn't it__?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'haven't you'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Question tags** turn a statement into a question. They are often used for checking information that we think we know is true.
 
• Usually, if the main clause is positive, the question tag is negative, and if the main clause is negative, the question tag is positive. **Both** the main clause and the question tag must be in the **same tense**. 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• It's cold (positive), isn't it (negative)?
 
• It isn't cold (negative), is it (positive)? 
 
 
 
• According to the given explanation, we can understand that **'haven't you'** is the correct usage. 
 
• Therefore, **option 3** is the correct answer.

questions.question:

I have __the bestest__ placement offer among all my classmates.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **the best**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the use of the non-standard word "**bestest**." 
 
• In formal or standard English, "**best**" is already the superlative form of "**good**," and adding "-**est**" to it creates redundancy.
 
• "**the best**" is grammatically correct and conveys the intended meaning effectively.
 
• It indicates that the speaker's placement offer is superior to those of their classmates.
 
• "**Best**" is the superlative form of the adjective "**good**," indicating the **highest level of quality**.

• "**Better**" is the comparative form of good, it doesn't fit well in this context.
 
• "**More**" is used to form the comparative degree of adjectives with more than one syllable (e.g., more beautiful, more intelligent).
 
• "**Good**" is a positive adjective, it doesn't convey the idea of superiority or excellence as effectively as "**the best**" does.
